planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into gritty, humus-enriched soil with sharp drainage, tucked into a rock garden crevice or raised bed where roots stay cool and moist but never waterlogged.

directions: Forrest's primrose is a compact, farina-dusted alpine primrose native to limestone cliffs and rocky woodland margins in Yunnan, China, where it wedges its rosettes into crevices with sharp drainage. In mid-to-late spring it sends up short stalks topped with a one-sided cluster of fragrant, bright yellow flowers held just above the silvery-mealy foliage. It thrives in gritty, humus-enriched soil that drains quickly yet never fully dries, and appreciates light shade from the hottest afternoon sun, especially outside its native cool, humid highland climate. Because the farina coating on the leaves washes off in heavy rain, a sheltered rock garden niche or alpine house helps the clumps persist for years.

planting.note: Divide and replant immediately after flowering into constantly moist, cool, humus-rich soil in a shaded woodland bed, raised trough, or alpine house pan.

directions: Gracilipes primrose is a dwarf Himalayan woodland species whose clusters of soft lilac-pink flowers sit tucked almost at ground level among farina-dusted rosettes, blooming in very early spring before taller companions emerge. In its native humid forests of Nepal, Sikkim, and Bhutan it grows in constantly moist, cool, humus-rich soil in dappled to full shade beneath deciduous canopy. Gardeners outside its native climate generally grow it in a shaded trough, raised bed, or alpine house where moisture can be kept constant without the soil ever becoming waterlogged or baking dry. Division of the rosettes right after flowering is the most reliable way to keep named forms true to type.

planting.note: Divide offsets just after bloom and replant in a raised, shaded woodland bed with gritty, humus-rich soil mulched in coarse grit around the crown to prevent winter rot.

directions: Griffith's primrose is a farina-coated Himalayan primrose from the high forests and scrub of Sikkim, Bhutan, and southeastern Tibet, producing dense, tightly packed heads of rich purple-violet flowers with a small yellow eye in early spring. Like other members of its Petiolares group, it demands constant moisture and cool, humus-rich soil but despises waterlogging, making a raised, shaded woodland bed or alpine house pan the most dependable home outside its native climate. Mulching with coarse grit around the crown helps prevent rot during wet winters while still conserving root moisture. It is slow to increase and best propagated by careful division of offsets immediately after bloom.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in bright shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs.

directions: 'Citronella' is a vigorous garden hybrid fawn lily descended from Erythronium tuolumnense, producing clear pale-yellow, down-facing flowers with gently reflexed petals held above handsomely mottled bronze-green leaves in early-to-mid spring. It is one of the easier Erythronium hybrids to grow and bulks up readily into sizeable clumps in a woodland setting, unlike many of the choosier Pacific Coast species it descends from. Plant the bulbs in fall beneath deciduous trees or shrubs where they receive bright shade and consistent spring moisture, then are allowed to dry down comfortably once the summer canopy closes overhead. It makes a reliable companion for other spring woodland bulbs and increases well by offsets over time.

subcategory: Pacific Northwest native shade spring bulb

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in partial to full shade, in colonies for best effect.

directions: This variety of the white fawn lily is distinguished from the typical form of Erythronium oregonum by its dark purple anthers rather than the cream-to-yellow anthers of var. oregonum, a small but reliable technical difference noted by Pacific Northwest botanists in populations scattered through parts of the species' Washington and Oregon range. Otherwise it shares the same reflexed, nodding white flowers with a yellow basal band and the same pair of handsomely mottled, bronze-and-silver leaves that emerge each spring from a deeply buried corm. It grows and is cultivated exactly like the typical variety, going fully dormant by midsummer, so it is best planted in drifts under deciduous trees where its disappearance after bloom goes unnoticed. Mark planting sites carefully, since no foliage marks the spot once the plant retreats underground for the year.
